claim: The majority of mitochondrial proteins are targeted to mitochondria by N-terminal presequences.
source: The majority of mitochondrial proteins are targeted to mitochondria by N-terminal presequences and use the TIM23 complex for their translocation across the mitochondrial inner membrane.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial protein targeting.

claim: Mitochondrial proteins targeted by N-terminal presequences use the TIM23 complex for their translocation across the mitochondrial inner membrane.
source: The majority of mitochondrial proteins are targeted to mitochondria by N-terminal presequences and use the TIM23 complex for their translocation across the mitochondrial inner membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the TIM23 complex function.

claim: During import, translocation through the channel in the inner membrane is coupled to the ATP-dependent action of an Hsp70-based import motor at the matrix face.
source: During import, translocation through the channel in the inner membrane is coupled to the ATP-dependent action of an Hsp70-based import motor at the matrix face.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial protein import mechanism.

claim: The N-terminal domain of Tim44 interacts with the components of the import motor.
source: The N-terminal domain of Tim44 interacts with the components of the import motor, whereas its C-terminal domain interacts with the translocation channel and is in contact with translocating proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the binding assays shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Tim44 interacts with the translocation channel.
source: The N-terminal domain of Tim44 interacts with the components of the import motor, whereas its C-terminal domain interacts with the translocation channel and is in contact with translocating proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the binding assays shown in Figure 6B demonstrating Tim17 binding.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Tim44 is in contact with translocating proteins.
source: The N-terminal domain of Tim44 interacts with the components of the import motor, whereas its C-terminal domain interacts with the translocation channel and is in contact with translocating proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by crosslinking and immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The translocation channel and the import motor of the TIM23 complex communicate through rearrangements of the two domains of Tim44.
source: Our data suggest that the translocation channel and the import motor of the TIM23 complex communicate through rearrangements of the two domains of Tim44 that are stimulated by translocating proteins.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rearrangements of the two domains of Tim44 are stimulated by translocating proteins.
source: Our data suggest that the translocation channel and the import motor of the TIM23 complex communicate through rearrangements of the two domains of Tim44 that are stimulated by translocating proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations but not directly demonstrated.

claim: Mitochondria import about 1000 different proteins synthesized as precursor proteins in the cytosol.

claim: Over half of mitochondrial proteins are synthesized with cleavable, N-terminal extensions called presequences.
source: Over half of mitochondrial proteins are synthesized with cleavable, N-terminal extensions called presequences.

source: Import of such precursor proteins requires a coordinated action of the TOM complex in the outer membrane and the TIM23 complex in the inner membrane and is driven by membrane potential across the inner membrane and ATP in the matrix (Dolezal et al., 2006; Endo et al., 2011; Koehler, 2004; Mokranjac and Neupert, 2009; Neupert and Herrmann, 2007; Schulz et al., 2015; Stojanovski et al., 2012).

claim: Import of presequence-containing precursor proteins is driven by membrane potential across the inner membrane.

claim: The TIM23 complex mediates translocation of presequence-containing precursor proteins into the matrix.

source: The latter process requires the presence of an additional, lateral insertion signal.

claim: Tim50 is a receptor of the TIM23 complex on the intermembrane space side of the inner membrane.
source: After initial recognition on the intermembrane space side of the inner membrane by the receptors of the TIM23 complex, Tim50 and Tim23, precursor proteins are transferred to the translocation channel in the inner membrane in a membrane-potential dependent step (Bajaj et al., 2014; Lytovchenko et al., 2013; Mokranjac et al., 2009; Shiota et al., 2011; Tamura et al., 2009).

claim: Multiple cycles of mtHsp70 binding to and release from translocating proteins are required for complete translocation across the inner membrane.
source: Multiple cycles of mtHsp70 binding to and release from translocating proteins are required for complete translocation across the inner membrane.

claim: The ATP hydrolysis-driven cycling of mtHsp70 is regulated by Tim14(Pam18).

claim: The ATP hydrolysis-driven cycling of mtHsp70 is regulated by Tim16(Pam16).
source: The ATP hydrolysis-driven cycling of mtHsp70 and thereby its binding to proteins is regulated by the J- and J-like proteins Tim14(Pam18) and Tim16(Pam16) as well as by the nucleotide-exchange factor Mge1 (D'Silva et al., 2003; Kozany et al., 2004; Mapa et al., 2010; Mokranjac et al., 2006; 2003b; Truscott et al., 2003).

claim: Tim44 recruits the Tim14-Tim16 subcomplex to mtHsp70.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

source: However, the C-terminal domain of Tim44 shows higher evolutionary conservation.

source: Still, the only function that has so far been attributed to the C-terminal domain is its role in recruitment of Tim44 to cardiolipin-containing membranes (Weiss et al., 1999).

claim: A surface-exposed hydrophobic cavity in the C-terminal domain was initially suggested to be important for membrane recruitment.
source: Based on the crystal structure of the C-terminal domain, a surface-exposed hydrophobic cavity was initially suggested to be important for membrane recruitment (Josyula et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Helices A1 and A2 (residues 235–262 in yeast Tim44) are important for membrane recruitment.
source: However, subsequent biochemical studies combined with molecular dynamics simulations, demonstrated that the helices A1 and A2 (residues 235–262 in yeast Tim44), present in the beginning of the C-terminal domain, are important for membrane recruitment (Marom et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of helices A1 and A2 abolished membrane association of the C-terminal domain.
source: Deletion of helices A1 and A2 abolished membrane association of the C-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature (Marom et al., 2009).

claim: Attachment of helices A1 and A2 to a soluble protein was sufficient to recruit it to a model membrane.
source: Interestingly, attachment of helices A1 and A2 to a soluble protein was sufficient to recruit it to a model membrane (Marom et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A construct consisting of the N-terminal domain of Tim44 extended to include the membrane-recruitment helices A1 and A2 is not sufficient to support the function of the full-length protein.
source: Upon incubation of transformed cells on a medium containing 5-fluoroorotic acid to remove the URA plasmid carrying the wild-type, full-length copy of Tim44, no viable cells were obtained (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Tim44 has a function beyond membrane recruitment that is essential for viability of yeast cells.
source: We conclude that the N-terminal domain of Tim44, even when extended to include the membrane-recruitment helices of the C-terminal domain, is not sufficient to support the function of the full-length protein. Furthermore, this result suggests that the C-terminal domain of Tim44 has a function beyond membrane recruitment that is apparently essential for viability of yeast cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing that the N-terminal domain with membrane recruitment helices cannot rescue viability.

claim: The function of Tim44 can be rescued by its two domains expressed in trans.
source: Surprisingly, we obtained viable colonies when both domains were expressed in the same cell but not when either of the two domains was expressed on its own (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The rescue of Tim44 function by its two domains expressed in trans is dependent on the presence of A1 and A2 helices on both domains.
source: The rescue was dependent on the presence of A1 and A2 helices on both domains (data not shown), as in their absence neither of the domains could even be stably expressed in yeast (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The two domains of Tim44, both carrying A1 and A2 helices, do not stably interact with each other in vitro.
source: However, we did not observe any copurification of the non-tagged C-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The two domains of Tim44 do not stably interact with each other in digitonin-solubilized mitochondria.
source: We also did not observe any stable interaction of the two domains when digitonin-solubilized mitochondria containing a His-tagged version of the N-terminal domain were used in a NiNTA pull-down experiment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The N+C strain grows relatively well on a fermentable carbon source at 24°C and 30°C.
source: The N+C strain was viable and grew relatively well on a fermentable carbon source at 24°C and 30°C (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The growth of the N+C strain is slower than that of the FL strain at 24°C and 30°C.
source: Still, its growth was slower than that of the FL strain at both temperatures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At 37°C, the N+C strain is barely viable.
source: At 37°C, the N+C strain was barely viable.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: N+C does not grow on a nonfermentable carbon source at any of the temperatures tested.
source: On a nonfermentable carbon source, when fully functional mitochondria are required, N+C did not grow at any of the temperatures tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The function of Tim44 can be reconstituted from its two domains separately, although only very poorly.
source: Thus, the function of Tim44 can be reconstituted from its two domains separately, although only very poorly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the growth data presented.

claim: N+C mitochondria contain no full-length Tim44 protein.
source: Immunostaining with antibodies raised against full-length Tim44 detected no full-length protein in N+C mitochondria but rather two faster migrating bands (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The endogenous levels of Tim17, Tim23, and Tim50 are not changed in N+C mitochondria compared to FL mitochondria.
source: The endogenous levels of other components of the TIM23 complex were either not changed at all (Tim17, Tim23, and Tim50), or were slightly upregulated (mtHsp70, Tim14, and Tim16), likely to compensate for only poorly functional Tim44.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The endogenous levels of mtHsp70, Tim14, and Tim16 are slightly upregulated in N+C mitochondria.
source: The endogenous levels of other components of the TIM23 complex were either not changed at all (Tim17, Tim23, and Tim50), or were slightly upregulated (mtHsp70, Tim14, and Tim16), likely to compensate for only poorly functional Tim44.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Upregulation of mtHsp70, Tim14, and Tim16 in N+C mitochondria likely compensates for only poorly functional Tim44.
source: The endogenous levels of other components of the TIM23 complex were either not changed at all (Tim17, Tim23, and Tim50), or were slightly upregulated (mtHsp70, Tim14, and Tim16), likely to compensate for only poorly functional Tim44.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed upregulation.

claim: Levels of Tom40, Tob55, and Tim22 are not altered in N+C mitochondria compared to FL mitochondria.
source: Levels of components of other essential mitochondrial protein translocases of the outer and inner mitochondrial membranes, Tom40, Tob55, and Tim22, were not altered compared to FL mitochondria.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When protein import into mitochondria is impaired, a precursor form of matrix-localized protein Mdj1 accumulates in vivo.
source: When import of precursor proteins into mitochondria is impaired, a precursor form of matrix-localized protein Mdj1 accumulates in vivo (Waegemann et al., 2015; Wrobel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A very prominent band of the precursor form of Mdj1 is observed in total cell extracts of N+C cells grown at 24°C and 30°C.
source: We indeed observed a very prominent band of the precursor form of Mdj1 in total cell extracts of N+C cells, grown at 24°C and 30°C, that was absent in cells containing full-length Tim44 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The efficiency of protein import into mitochondria is reduced in N+C cells.
source: Thus, the efficiency of protein import into mitochondria is reduced in N+C cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the accumulation of precursor Mdj1.

claim: The import efficiencies of pF1β, pcytb2(1–167)△DHFR, and pSu9(1–69)DHFR are drastically reduced in N+C mitochondria compared to wild type.
source: The import efficiencies of all matrix-targeted precursors analyzed, pF1β, pcytb2(1–167)△DHFR, and pSu9(1–69)DHFR, were drastically reduced in N+C mitochondria when compared to wild type.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: Import of presequence-containing precursor of Oxa1 is impaired in N+C mitochondria.
source: Import of presequence-containing precursor of Oxa1 that contains multiple transmembrane segments was similarly impaired.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Precursor proteins pDLD1 and pcytb2 that are laterally inserted into the inner membrane by the TIM23 complex are imported with reduced efficiency into N+C mitochondria.
source: Likewise, precursor proteins that are laterally inserted into the inner membrane by the TIM23 complex, such as pDLD1 and pcytb2, were imported with reduced efficiency into N+C mitochondria.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: N+C mitochondria have a slightly reduced membrane potential compared to wild type.
source: In agreement with the established role of Tim44 in import of precursors of a number of components of respiratory chain complexes and their assembly factors, we observed a slightly reduced membrane potential in N+C mitochondria as compared to wild type (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Precursors of ATP/ADP carrier and of Tim23 are imported with similar efficiencies in both FL and N+C mitochondria.
source: However, precursors of ATP/ADP carrier and of Tim23, whose imports into mitochondria are not dependent on the TIM23 complex, were imported with similar efficiencies in both types of mitochondria, demonstrating that observed effects are not due to general dysfunction of mitochondria.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I-J.

claim: Splitting of Tim44 into two domains in N+C cells severely impairs transport of proteins by the TIM23 complex.
source: We conclude that splitting of Tim44 into two domains in N+C cells severely impairs transport of proteins by the TIM23 complex, suggesting that full-length Tim44 is required for efficient import of presequence-containing precursor proteins into mitochondria.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the import data presented.

claim: Full-length Tim44 is required for efficient import of presequence-containing precursor proteins into mitochondria.
source: We conclude that splitting of Tim44 into two domains in N+C cells severely impairs transport of proteins by the TIM23 complex, suggesting that full-length Tim44 is required for efficient import of presequence-containing precursor proteins into mitochondria.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the import data presented.

claim: The TIM23 complex is properly assembled in N+C mitochondria.
source: We observed essentially the same precipitation pattern when we analyzed digitonin-solubilized N+C mitochondria, demonstrating that the TIM23 complex is properly assembled.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both N and C domains of Tim44 are recruited to the TIM23 complex in N+C mitochondria.
source: Importantly, both N and C domains of Tim44 were recruited to the TIM23 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In wild-type mitochondria, Tim16 can be crosslinked to mtHsp70, Tim44, and Tim14 in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: In wild-type mitochondria, Tim16 can be crosslinked to mtHsp70, Tim44, and Tim14 in an ATP-dependent manner (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In N+C mitochondria, Tim16 can be crosslinked to mtHsp70 and to Tim14.
source: In N+C mitochondria, the same crosslinks of Tim16 to mtHsp70 and to Tim14 were observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A crosslink between two Tim16 molecules becomes prominent in N+C mitochondria.
source: In addition, a crosslink between two Tim16 molecules became prominent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A Tim16 dimer crosslink has previously been observed in mutants in which conformation of the TIM23 complex was altered.
source: Interestingly, this crosslink has previously been observed in mutants in which conformation of the TIM23 complex was altered (Popov-Čeleketić et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A prominent Tim23-dimer crosslink appears in N+C mitochondria.
source: In addition to the crosslink of Tim23 to Pam17, observed in both FL and N+C mitochondria, a prominent Tim23-dimer crosslink appeared in N+C mitochondria.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The conformation of the TIM23 complex is changed in N+C mitochondria.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that the conformation of the TIM23 complex is changed in N+C mitochondria.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the crosslinking and BN-PAGE data.

claim: Alterations in the components traditionally assigned to the import motor affect the conformation of the translocation channel in the inner membrane.
source: They further show that alterations in the components traditionally assigned to the import motor affect the conformation of the translocation channel in the inner membrane, supporting the notion of an intricate crosstalk within the complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed conformational changes.

claim: mtHsp70, Tim16, Tim14, and Tim17 bind to full-length Tim44.
source: We observed prominent, specific binding of mtHsp70, Tim16, Tim14 and Tim17, and to a far lesser degree of Tim23 and Tim50, to full-length Tim44 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: mtHsp70, Tim16, and Tim14 efficiently bind to the N-terminal domain of Tim44.
source: mtHsp70, Tim16 and Tim14 also efficiently bound to the N-terminal domain of Tim44, in agreement with previous observations (Schilke et al., 2012; Schiller et al., 2008), and far less efficiently to the C-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and citations to previous literature.

claim: Binding of Tim17 to the N-terminal domain of Tim44 is drastically lower compared to its binding to the full-length protein.
source: Binding of Tim17 to the N-terminal domain of Tim44 was drastically lower compared to its binding to the full-length protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A strong binding of Tim17 to the C-terminal domain of Tim44 was observed.
source: Instead, a strong binding of Tim17 to the C-terminal domain of Tim44 was observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The N-terminal domain of Tim44 binds to the components of the import motor.
source: We conclude that the N-terminal domain of Tim44 binds to the components of the import motor, whereas the C-terminal domain binds to the translocation channel in the inner membrane, revealing a novel function of the C-terminal domain of Tim44.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the binding data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Tim44 binds to the translocation channel in the inner membrane.
source: We conclude that the N-terminal domain of Tim44 binds to the components of the import motor, whereas the C-terminal domain binds to the translocation channel in the inner membrane, revealing a novel function of the C-terminal domain of Tim44.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the binding data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Tim44 is in close vicinity of the translocating protein.
source: This demonstrates that the C-terminal domain of Tim44 is in close vicinity of the translocating protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by crosslinking and immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Pro308Gln mutation in human Tim44 has been linked to oncocytic thyroid carcinoma.
source: In this respect, Pro308Gln mutation in human Tim44 has recently been linked to oncocytic thyroid carcinoma (Bonora et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The melting temperature of wild-type Tim44 is 54°C.
source: The melting temperature of wild-type Tim44 was 54°C, whereas that of the mutant protein was 4°C lower (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The melting temperature of Pro282Gln mutant Tim44 is 4°C lower than wild-type.
source: The melting temperature of wild-type Tim44 was 54°C, whereas that of the mutant protein was 4°C lower (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The Pro282Gln mutation significantly destabilizes Tim44.
source: This demonstrates that the mutation significantly destabilizes Tim44, providing first clues toward molecular understanding of the associated human disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the thermal shift assay data.

claim: Tim44 holds the TIM23 complex together through its two domains having different interaction partners.
source: We show here that the two domains of Tim44 have different interaction partners within the TIM23 complex. In this way, Tim44 holds the TIM23 complex together.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the binding data presented.

claim: There is a direct interaction between the C-terminal domain of Tim44 with the channel component Tim17.
source: Our data revealed a direct, previously unexpected interaction between the C-terminal domain of Tim44 with the channel component Tim17.
evidence: This claim is supported by the binding data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The two currently available crystal structures of the C-terminal domains of yeast and human Tim44s showed different orientations of the two helices relative to the core domains.
source: Intriguingly, the two currently available crystal structures of the C-terminal domains of yeast and human Tim44s showed different orientations of the two helices relative to the core domains (Handa et al., 2007; Josyula et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The conformational change in the C-terminal domain of Tim44 was likely induced upon PEG binding during crystallization.
source: The conformational change was likely induced upon PEG binding to this region of human Tim44 during crystallization (Handa et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The same conformational change observed in crystal structures may take place during translocation of proteins in the mitochondria.
source: It is tempting to speculate that the same conformational change takes place during translocation of proteins in the mitochondria.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observations.

claim: There is a very strong evolutionary pressure to keep the two domains of Tim44 within one polypeptide chain.
source: Also, there is obviously a very strong evolutionary pressure to keep the two domains of Tim44 within one polypeptide chain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evolutionary conservation and the poor function of split domains.

claim: N+C strain had to be kept at all times on the selective medium.
source: N+C strain had to be kept at all times on the selective medium - even after only an overnight incubation on a nonselective medium the full-length protein reappeared (our unpublished observation), likely due to a recombination event between two plasmids.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Tim44 can be crosslinked to translocating proteins.
source: Tim44 can be crosslinked to translocating proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: A direct interaction of the C-terminal domain of Tim44 with Tim17 would optimally position the C-terminal domain to the outlet of the translocation channel.
source: A direct interaction of the same domain with Tim17 would optimally position the C-terminal domain to the outlet of the translocation channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding data and known structure of the TIM23 complex.

claim: Translocating precursor proteins may play an important role in conformational changes of Tim44.
source: This raises an interesting possibility that translocating precursor proteins may play an important role in the above postulated conformational changes of Tim44.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data presented.

claim: The Pro282Gln mutation in yeast Tim44 produced no obvious growth phenotype or an in vivo import defect.
source: The corresponding mutation in yeast, Pro282Gln, destabilized the protein but produced no obvious growth phenotype or an in vivo import defect (our unpublished observations), suggesting that the yeast system is more robust.
evidence: This is based on unpublished experimental observations.

claim: The yeast system is more robust than the human system with respect to Tim44 mutations.
source: The corresponding mutation in yeast, Pro282Gln, destabilized the protein but produced no obvious growth phenotype or an in vivo import defect (our unpublished observations), suggesting that the yeast system is more robust.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of yeast and human phenotypes.

claim: Mutations that would severely affect the function of the TIM23 complex would likely be embryonically lethal in humans.
source: This observation is in agreement with the notion that mutations that would severely affect the function of the TIM23 complex would likely be embryonically lethal in humans.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the importance of the TIM23 complex.

claim: The Pro308Gln mutation in human Tim44 maps to the short loop between A3 and A4 helices in the C-terminal domain.
source: Furthermore, the mutation maps to the short loop between A3 and A4 helices in the C-terminal domain of Tim44.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of Tim44.

claim: The Pro308Gln mutation could affect the conformational flexibility of the A1 and A2 helices.
source: Based on the crystal structure of Tim44, it was previously suggested that the mutation could affect the conformational flexibility of the A1 and A2 helices (Handa et al., 2007), intriguingly providing further support for the above postulated conformational changes of Tim44.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the resting state, the translocation channel is closed to maintain the permeability barrier of the inner membrane.
source: In the resting state, the translocation channel is closed to maintain the permeability barrier of the inner membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about membrane channels.

claim: During translocation of proteins, the translocation channel in the inner membrane has to open to allow passage of proteins.
source: During translocation of proteins (2), the translocation channel in the inner membrane has to open to allow passage of proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein translocation.

claim: Opening of the channel will likely change the conformation of Tim17.
source: Opening of the channel will likely change the conformation of Tim17 that could be further conveyed to the C-terminal domain Tim44.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the model proposed.

claim: Conformational change in Tim17 could be conveyed to the C-terminal domain of Tim44.
source: Opening of the channel will likely change the conformation of Tim17 that could be further conveyed to the C-terminal domain Tim44.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the model proposed.

claim: Conformational change is transduced to the N-terminal domain of Tim44 through the central, membrane-bound segment of Tim44.
source: It is tempting to speculate that this conformational change is transduced to the N-terminal domain of Tim44 through the central, membrane-bound segment of Tim44, leading to relative rearrangements of the two domains of Tim44.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the model proposed.

claim: The release of mtHsp70 with bound polypeptide from the N-terminal domain of Tim44 will send a signal back to the C-terminal domain of Tim44 and further to the translocation channel.
source: We speculate that the release of mtHsp70 with bound polypeptide from the N-terminal domain of Tim44 will send a signal back to the C-terminal domain of Tim44 and further to the translocation channel.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the model proposed.

claim: Multiple cycles of mtHsp70 are required to translocate the entire polypeptide chain into the matrix.
source: Multiple cycles of mtHsp70 are required to translocate the entire polypeptide chain into the matrix.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mtHsp70-driven translocation.
